=> 7
--- check case | Walls force a detour
collect_all(["S#*", ".#.", "..."])
=> 6
--- check case | No samples, and a sample behind walls
(collect_all(["..S.."]), collect_all(["S.#*"]))
=> (0, -1)
--- check case | The nearest sample first is not the best order
collect_all(["*.S*.*"])
=> 7
--- check case | A 40 by 40 map with 12 samples
collect_all((lambda P: ["".join("S" if (r, c) == (0, 0) else "*" if (r, c) in P else "#" if (r * 7 + c * 11) % 13 == 5 else "." for c in range(40)) for r in range(40)])({(3, 37), (38, 2), (20, 20), (10, 5), (33, 30), (5, 25), (25, 8), (15, 33), (39, 39), (0, 39), (39, 0), (28, 18)}))
=> 190

+++ question | Dijkstra with one negative edge
--- ask
Dijkstra's algorithm, which finalises each vertex the first time it leaves the heap and never changes it again, runs on a directed graph where every edge cost is positive except one edge of cost −5. There is no negative cycle. What can happen?
--- choice
It still returns correct distances, because there is no negative cycle.
--- choice correct
It can return a wrong distance: a vertex is finalised when it leaves the heap, and a cheaper route to it that uses the negative edge may be found only later.
--- choice
It loops forever, because the negative edge keeps lowering distances.
--- choice
It crashes, because the heap cannot hold negative numbers.
--- why
Dijkstra's correctness argument says: when a vertex has the smallest tentative distance, no route through vertices not yet finalised can be cheaper, because every extra edge only adds cost. A negative edge breaks exactly that step. For example, with edges s→a of cost 2, s→b of cost 5 and b→a of cost −5, Dijkstra finalises a at 2 before it looks at b, but the route s, b, a costs 0. Without negative cycles, Bellman-Ford gives the right answer in O(n · m), and with a negative cycle there is no shortest route at all. Heaps hold negative numbers without any trouble.

+++ question | The order of the loops in Floyd-Warshall
--- ask
Floyd-Warshall is written with three nested loops over k, i and j, and the update `d[i][j] = min(d[i][j], d[i][k] + d[k][j])`. Why must the loop over k be the **outer** one?
--- choice correct
Its invariant is "after round k, d[i][j] is the shortest path whose middle vertices all come from the first k vertices". Round k builds on the finished round k − 1 for every pair, so every pair must be updated for one k before moving on to the next.
--- choice
Because the loop over k is the fastest to run, and the fastest loop should be outside.
--- choice
Any order gives the same answer; putting k outside is only a convention.
--- choice
Because k must count down from n − 1 to 0, and only the outer loop can count down.
--- why
The DP state is "shortest i-to-j path using only vertices 0 to k in between". A path through k is a best path from i to k plus a best path from k to j, both using only vertices before k, which round k − 1 has already finished for **all** pairs. With k innermost, d[i][j] would be finalised after looking at each k once, using entries that were not yet complete, and some shortest paths are missed. The order of i and j inside does not matter.

+++ question | A heuristic that overestimates
--- ask
A* search on a grid uses a heuristic h(v) that sometimes **overestimates** the true remaining distance to the goal. What can happen?
--- choice
A* becomes faster and still finds a shortest path.
--- choice correct
A* can return a path that is longer than the shortest one, because a vertex on the best path may look too expensive and be left in the queue while the goal is reached another way.
--- choice
A* can fail to find any path, even though one exists.
--- choice
Nothing changes: A* always finds a shortest path, whatever h is.
--- why
A* expands vertices in order of g + h, the cost so far plus the estimate. If h never overestimates (it is admissible), then when the goal leaves the queue, no unexplored route can be cheaper, so the path is optimal. An overestimate can make the true best route look worse than a poor one, and A* stops at the goal with the poor one. It still finds *a* path whenever one exists, since it keeps exploring until the goal leaves the queue. Overestimating heuristics are sometimes used on purpose, to trade optimality for speed.

+++ question | Bits after Huffman coding
--- ask
The message `aaaaabbcd` (five `a`, two `b`, one `c`, one `d`) is encoded with a Huffman code built from exactly these counts. How many bits long is the encoded message? Type the number.
--- answer
15
--- why
Huffman merges the two lightest trees each time: c (1) and d (1) make 2; then b (2) and that 2 make 4; then a (5) and 4 make 9. So a gets a 1-bit code, b a 2-bit code, and c and d 3-bit codes. The total is 5 · 1 + 2 · 2 + 1 · 3 + 1 · 3 = 15 bits. Ties among equal weights can change which codes you get, but never the total length, which is the minimum possible for any prefix code with these counts. A fixed-length code would need 2 bits per symbol, 18 bits in all.

+++ question | Why earliest finish time
--- ask
To choose the most talks that do not overlap from a list of talks with start and end times, the greedy algorithm repeatedly takes the talk that **ends earliest** among those compatible with the talks already taken. Why that rule, and not "take the shortest talk"?
--- choice correct
Exchange argument: an optimal schedule can swap its first talk for the talk that ends earliest, without clashing with the rest, because that talk ends no later. Repeating the swap turns any optimal schedule into the greedy one. A short talk can sit across two talks that together fit.
--- choice
Both rules always give the same number of talks; ending earliest is just easier to code.
--- choice
Shortest-first is correct too, but slower, because it needs a heap.
--- choice
The talk ending earliest is always the shortest one, so the two rules are the same.
--- why
Take any optimal schedule and look at its first talk. The greedy's first talk ends at or before it, so replacing one with the other keeps the schedule valid and just as long. By induction on the rest, the greedy schedule is as long as the optimal one. Shortest-first fails on talks [0, 10), [9, 12) and [11, 20): the shortest, [9, 12), clashes with both others, so shortest-first gets 1 talk while earliest-end gets 2.

+++ question | The prefix function of a pattern
--- ask
KMP's prefix function gives, for each position i of the pattern, the length of the longest proper prefix of `pattern[0..i]` that is also a suffix of it. What is the prefix function of `aabaaab`? Type the seven numbers separated by spaces.
--- answer
0 1 0 1 2 2 3
0, 1, 0, 1, 2, 2, 3
[0, 1, 0, 1, 2, 2, 3]
0,1,0,1,2,2,3
--- why
Position by position: `a` has no proper prefix, 0. `aa` ends with `a`, 1. `aab` has no border, 0. `aaba` ends with `a`, 1. `aabaa` ends with `aa`, 2. `aabaaa`: the border `aab` would need a `b` next, so fall back to the border of `aa`, which is `a`, then extend to `aa`: 2. `aabaaab` ends with `aab`, 3. These values let KMP shift the pattern after a mismatch without ever moving backwards in the text, which is why matching is O(n + m).

+++ question | Sparse tables and sums
--- ask
A sparse table answers range-minimum queries on a fixed array in O(1) time, by combining two precomputed blocks whose lengths are a power of two and which may overlap. Why can the same trick not answer range-**sum** queries in O(1)?
--- choice
Because sums can overflow, while minimums cannot.
--- choice correct
Minimum is idempotent: counting an element twice does not change the minimum. Two overlapping blocks count the overlap twice, which is harmless for min but wrong for a sum.
--- choice
Because a sparse table stores only the positions of minimums, not values.
--- choice
It can: a sparse table answers range sums in O(1) too, as long as the array does not change.
--- why
For a query on [l, r], take k as the largest power of two with 2^k ≤ r − l + 1. The blocks starting at l and ending at r, each of length 2^k, cover the range, usually overlapping in the middle. min(a, a) = a, so the overlap does no harm. For sums you would have to split the range into disjoint power-of-two blocks, which takes O(log n) of them, or better, use prefix sums, which answer static range sums in O(1) with subtraction, an inverse that min does not have.

+++ question | The lowest bit
--- ask
What does this print? Type the output exactly.

```python
x = 44
print(x & -x, bin(x & (x - 1)))
```
--- answer
4 0b101000
--- why
44 is 101100 in binary. `-x` is `~x + 1`, which flips every bit above the lowest 1 and keeps that 1, so `x & -x` is just the lowest 1: 100, which is 4. `x - 1` turns the lowest 1 into 0 and the zeros below it into 1s: 101011. ANDing with x clears exactly that lowest 1: 101000, printed by `bin` as `0b101000`, which is 40.

+++ question | An inverse modulo 26
--- ask
Using extended Euclid, find the inverse of 7 modulo 26: the number x from 0 to 25 with 7 · x ≡ 1 (mod 26). Type the number.
--- answer
15
--- why
Euclid on 26 and 7: 26 = 3 · 7 + 5, 7 = 1 · 5 + 2, 5 = 2 · 2 + 1. Working back: 1 = 5 − 2 · 2 = 5 − 2 · (7 − 5) = 3 · 5 − 2 · 7 = 3 · (26 − 3 · 7) − 2 · 7 = 3 · 26 − 11 · 7. So 7 · (−11) ≡ 1 (mod 26), and −11 mod 26 is 15. Check: 7 · 15 = 105 = 4 · 26 + 1. The inverse exists because gcd(7, 26) = 1; 13 would have none modulo 26.

+++ question | Proving a new problem hard
--- ask
You meet a new problem X and suspect it is NP-hard. Which of these proves it (assuming the transformation runs in polynomial time and preserves yes and no answers)?
--- choice
Transform every instance of X into an instance of 3-SAT.
--- choice correct
Transform every instance of 3-SAT (or another NP-complete problem) into an instance of X.
--- choice
Show that X has no polynomial algorithm on a few hard-looking examples.
--- choice
Show that a certificate for X can be checked in polynomial time.
--- why
A reduction from A to B shows B is at least as hard as A: a fast algorithm for B would solve A. So to show X is hard, reduce a known NP-complete problem **to** X. Reducing X to 3-SAT shows only that X is no harder than 3-SAT, which is true of every problem in NP. A polynomial verifier shows X is in NP, the other half of NP-completeness, and examples prove nothing about all inputs.

+++ question | Why taking both ends is at most twice the best
--- ask
The vertex cover approximation goes through the edges and, for each edge with neither end covered, adds both ends. Why is its cover never more than twice the size of the smallest cover?
--- choice
Because every vertex it adds has at least one edge, and a smallest cover needs at least one vertex per edge.
--- choice correct
The edges it picks share no endpoints (a matching), and any cover must contain a different vertex for each of them. So the smallest cover has at least as many vertices as picked edges, and the algorithm adds exactly two per picked edge.
--- choice
Because it adds vertices in order of degree, and high-degree vertices are in every smallest cover.
--- choice
It is not: on a star graph it can add every leaf, far more than twice the best.
--- why
Once an edge is picked, both its ends are covered, so no later picked edge can touch them: the picked edges form a matching M. A cover must hit every edge of M, and no vertex hits two of them, so OPT ≥ |M|, while the algorithm returns 2|M|. On a star, the first edge covers the centre, and every other edge is then already covered, so the algorithm returns just 2 vertices. The ratio 2 is tight on a graph made of one edge.
